title: Saleor Dashboard: customer types management (#6856, #6867, #6876)
source: Three merged changes, 24 to 27 August 2026, applied alone on the commit before the first: 14,293 lines added in 237 files, 41 of them test files.
notes:
# Working in this environment

- Node 24 and pnpm are installed. The project's dependencies are installed at `/deps/node_modules`, and `node_modules` here is a link to them. There is no internet: nothing can be installed.
- Run tests with `npx jest <path>`, for example `npx jest src/customers`. The whole suite (`npx jest --silent --maxWorkers=4`) is about 830 files and takes three minutes.
- The GraphQL schema of the API this dashboard calls is kept here as copies: `schema-main.graphql` and `schema-staging.graphql` (`schema.graphql` is a link to the first). Typed query code under `src/graphql/*.generated.ts` is generated from those copies and from the queries in `src/**/queries.ts`, `src/**/mutations.ts`, `src/fragments/*.ts` and `src/searches/*.ts`: run `pnpm run generate` after changing either (a few seconds).
- `API_URL=http://<host>:8000/graphql/ pnpm run fetch-local-schema` writes the schema a running API serves into `schema.graphql`.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` checks types (several minutes).
- A shell command is stopped after 180 seconds. Start anything longer in the background and read its log: `nohup npx jest --silent --maxWorkers=4 > /tmp/jest.log 2>&1 &`.
- There is no git history.
brief:
You are working in the Saleor Dashboard, the staff application of the Saleor commerce platform (TypeScript, React), at the commit before a feature was added. Build that feature: customer types and customer attributes.

Saleor's API is gaining customer types: customers can be grouped into types, each with its own set of attributes, the way products have product types. The dashboard must let staff use it. The project describes the work like this:

1. Configuration has a new **Customers** section with **Customer types** and **Customer attributes**. A customer type defines the attributes its customers share, so details like tax ID, account manager, or contract tier live on the profile as proper fields instead of metadata or free-text notes. Types can be created, renamed, given a default, and have attributes assigned, reordered, or unassigned, the same way product and model types work.
2. On a customer profile you can pick the type, fill in its attributes, and jump to the type's settings from the attributes card. The type also appears as a badge in the profile header, linking to that type's tab on the customer list. The customer list uses type tabs (like models) and the current `where` API for other filters.
3. The customer detail page is reorganised around this: the header carries status, type, and member-since; the main column shows channel-scoped order KPIs, recent orders, and attributes; contact details, addresses, external reference, and gift cards sit in the sidebar. Recent orders rows are clickable across the full row.
4. Customer types are in the Customers sidebar. Open **Customers** to jump to **All**, or to a type such as **B2B** or **Default**. **Customer Types** at the bottom opens the type settings. If there is only one type, the menu stays **All** plus settings. Types pinned on the customer list appear first; only a handful of types are listed so the menu stays short.
5. Customers can be filtered by attributes: on the customer list, open **Conditions** and choose **Attribute**. Filter menus show more choices and load on scroll.

The dashboard's copies of the API schema do not describe customer types yet: the API side of this feature is being built at the same time, in the API's own repository. The dashboard must call the API as it is really built.

The work is judged by the project's own tests for this feature, which you cannot see, and by whether every GraphQL operation the dashboard sends is valid against the API as built. `NOTES.md` says how to work here, and `INTERFACE.md` lists the file and export names those tests use.

exact: The copies of the API's schema kept here describe the API as it is today, without the feature. They are judged as well: they must state what the API gained, exactly as the API's code produces it.

`src/customerTypes/components/CustomerTypeTabs/CustomerTypeTabs.tsx` exports `CustomerTypeTabs`, and `src/customerTypes/components/CustomerTypeDetails/CustomerTypeDetails.tsx` exports `CustomerTypeDetails` (named exports; the tests mock both by these names).

`src/customers/hooks/useCustomerDetailsAttributes.ts` exports `useCustomerDetailsAttributes`, which returns `{ attributeRichTextGetters, attributes, attributeValues, fetchAttributeValues, fetchMoreAttributeValues, getSubmitData, handleTypeChange, isDirty, handlers: { fetchMoreReferences, fetchReferences, onAttributeSelectBlur, onChange, onFileChange, onMultiChange, onReferencesReorder, selectAttributeReference, selectAttributeReferenceAdditionalData }, typeAttributesLoading }`; `getSubmitData()` resolves to `{ attributes, attributesWithNewFileValue }`. The customer details page uses it; its test mocks it with that shape.
The query of customer types the customer's attributes card uses is named `CustomerTypeList` (so its hook is `useCustomerTypeListQuery`; the card's test mocks it).

When a customer's type is changed to one with different attributes, the attributes card says "This type uses different attributes" and "Values from the previous type stay stored. They'll show again if you switch back."

When the customer list is filtered to one customer type (`CustomerListPage` props `selectedTypeIds` and `activeCustomerTypeName`), its create button is labelled "Create " and the type's name, for example "Create B2B".
